title: How the word 'jazz' was attached to Tom Brown's band
summary: Allen and Wiggs say the name was put on Tom Brown's band in Chicago to hurt it but it backfired; Chance makes peace.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yes, sir. Let's get a comment from Mr. Wiggs in here.
Well, I tell you, the gentleman said so many things, I really wouldn't know where to start on.

Well, one thing that struck me is we were really talking about the word jazz, how it got applied. And I think Eddie Chance's uncle had documents, which, as far as anybody knows now, prove that jazz was first applied to his band up in Chicago. It was a New Orleans band that went to Chicago, and they had to stick a name on it. So they put the word jazz on it. That was Tom Brown's band.

Yeah, they put that name on to hurt the band. Of course, the word jazz has an ugly meaning, and that's the reason they put the word on Tom Brown's band, who was a perfectly innocent purveyor of music. And instead of doing him harm, everybody wanted to hear that kind of music, which is called jazz. That's for all it wasn't, huh?
Mr. Chance, we thank you for calling. We have to go into what we call a station break here.

Thank you very much. Well, I'm sorry, because I really like to, I have a lot of condensals to prove what I have said and tell Johnny and Steve Allen that I didn't mean any harm to them, because I like Johnny. I have played with Johnny a long time, and he's a wonderful trumpet player. I just wanted to get that straight about that jazz proposition, because there's too many people trying to claim it. It's only claimed by the boys, just like Johnny said. Johnny's correct. They thought they would hate the band, but instead of that, they made a big thing out of it.
Right, so everybody will go away friends except Mr. Allen, who you called Steve. It's Dick. Thank you for calling.
